author: Valerie Anne
title: ‘The Body’ Is a Sapphic, Ritual-Gone-Wrong Teen Horror Show Coming to Netflix
content:
Do you ever feel like a show was made just for you using all your favorite media keywords? That’s how I felt when I first heard about Netflix’s The Body. I saw Catholic school, dancers, ritual-gone-wrong, horror and I was beyond sold.

And in case those words and phrases didn’t make it obvious: The story is also sapphic. Writer and creator Quinn Shephard (who acted in movies like The Miseducation of Cameron Post and wrote/directed episodes of Under the Bridge) started writing the show the year she came out. She says: “It’s satirizing some of the trauma of growing up queer and repressed and the confusion around that.”

A lot of the main cast of girls are relative newcomers on the scene (aka they don’t have Wikipedia “personal life” pages yet) so I’m not sure who among them are queer, but the show WILL feature lesbian reality star Gabby Windey in a recurring role as a coach. Also, almost all of the episodes have women listed as writers.

The show looks freaky and weird in all the best ways, and I can’t wait. I hope it’s just as fun as shows like Yellowjackets and even Mike Flanagan’s Carrie. May the teens-getting-into-supernatural-mischief genre never die.

The series drops next month and you can watch the full official trailer right now!

title: Horror Comedy ‘The Blood Countess’ Imagines Elizabeth Báthory as a Lesbian Vampire
content:
If I had a nickel for every piece of queer media about 17th century Hungarian countess Elizabeth Báthory released this year, I’d have two nickels. Which isn’t a lot, but it’s weird that it happened twice. After her strange appearance in Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, she also appears in the vampire horror comedy The Blood Countess directed and co-written by lesbian filmmaker Ulrike Ottinger. In the film, Báthory (played by Isabelle Huppert) wakes from a long slumber and finds herself in modern-day Vienna, searching for a book that could cure her vampirism.

I find two things interesting about the fact that the countess has appeared in two queer adaptations this year. The first is that Lizzie Borden actually never really portrayed her as a lesbian, even though she was set up parallel to Lizzie and lesbian serial killer Aileen Wuornos and was played by the same actress who played Lizzie’s lover. Before the much-later rumors that Elizabeth Báthory bathed in the blood of virgin girls, the crimes she was accused of were more along the lines of torture and cannibalism. So it’s interesting that was then interpreted as lesbianism. Then again, she was luring young women to her castle with three of her closest gal pals, so, who knows I guess. author: Valerie Anne
title: Lili Reinhart Wants To Adapt a Lesbian Vampire Novella — Let Her!
content:
feature image photo by Emma McIntyre / Staff via Getty Images

Bisexual baddie Lili Reinhart has been on a press tour for her new film, The Love Hypothesis, and I’ve been really enjoying her interviews. The film seems to be the CLASSIC fake dating trope come to life — in fact, the book it’s based on started as Star Wars fanfic! — and despite the movie being seemingly extremely heterosexual, on this tour, she has been quick to remind interviewers and fans that she’s queer. She has also said she hopes in her next project is gay. (Fingers crossed!)

In one video interview she says, “I’m instantly way more interested in doing a movie if my character is a little gay,” she continued. “Because I’m a little gay.” She also reads a comment about being one of “the five pillars of bisexuality with preference to women” and she called it an honor.

In that same interview, she also mentioned that she’s trying to get a film adaptation of a lesbian vampire novella made but that Hollywood seems “too afraid” to make it. She also wonders aloud who WOULDN’T want to make it, a sentiment I agree with. The general assumption people have been making is that it would be an adaptation of the 1872 novella Carmilla, which the popular webseries starring Natasha Negovanlis and Elise Bauman was based on, and I think that would be fun if true. title: ‘Practical Magic 2’ Straightwashed Its Lesbian but Maisie Williams Played Her Gay Anyway
content:
Leading up to the release of Practical Magic 2, we were all hoping this witchy sequel would be even gayer than the gay undertones of the first because, in the source material, Sally Owens’ daughter Antonia is a lesbian. And while there were potentially versions of the movie that expressed that, the final edit left Antonia’s sexuality undetermined. However, Maisie Williams has been sure to tell everyone on the press tour that she knew the source material and regardless of what the final edit revealed, she played Antonia as a “sapphic icon” and that it brought some nuance to certain scenes since it meant Antonia had a different perspective on men than the other women in her family.

This is a shame and not the first time queerness in a book has been watered down or erased altogether in their adaptations. To name a few: Fried Green Tomatoes, The Color Purple, and don’t even get me started on comic book characters that are queer on the page but straight on screen. Studios are cowards and it’s the same reason queer storylines are often cut from animated films, or even single lines in big box office hits that would mean a lot to the queer community but scare the money men.
